correctness.rationale: For each matching index \(j\), comparing a clique vertex \(a_i\) with the clique edge \(a_i a_j\) for \(i\ne j\) shows that only \(a_j\) or \(b_j\) can distinguish them, forcing every mixed generator to meet each matching pair and hence have size at least \(n\). Equality is therefore a matching transversal. A transversal with fewer than two selected vertices in either clique layer creates an explicit vertex-edge or edge-edge collision. When both layers contribute at least two selections, the exact zero-distance and distance-two index sets determine every vertex and edge; the only possible cross-layer clique-edge ambiguity would require exactly two selections in each layer, hence \(n=4\), which is excluded. A fresh direct mixed-distance enumeration for \(n=5\) found exactly 20 bases, agreeing with \(2^5-10-2\), and the frozen verifier exhausts \(5\le n\le9\).
correctness.risk: The stable classification starts at \(n=5\); the \(n=4\) boundary genuinely behaves differently.

value.rationale: \(K_n\square K_2\) is a basic Cartesian-product family. The theorem supplies not only the exact mixed metric dimension but every optimum basis and its count, with a sharp explanation of the exceptional \(n=4\) boundary. This is a natural reusable product-graph benchmark.
value.risk: No claim is made for general \(K_m\square K_n\).

final_claim: For the complete prism \(K_n\square K_2\) with \(n\ge5\), the mixed metric dimension is \(n\); the mixed metric bases are exactly the matching transversals choosing one endpoint from every matching pair and at least two chosen vertices in each clique layer; hence there are \(2^n-2n-2\) bases.
limitations: The \(n=4\) case has a different minimum behavior and is excluded.
